sections.heading: Client Updates
sections.summary: Lighthouse enabled partial data columns on mainnet by default; Geth updated blsync for Glamsterdam; Nethermind added a CL plugin and is researching a light client.
sections.body:
- Lighthouse released on Monday with partial data columns (partial messages) enabled on mainnet by default; usage rate expected to rise as operators deploy the update.
  - Mainnet has not broken since the release; metrics to be shared at the next networking call.
- Partial data columns allow nodes to communicate only missing blobs rather than re-gossiping full columns, reducing waste when most blobs are already known via the public mempool (getBlobs V3/V4).
  - Mechanism is gossip-like but closer to an RPC pull structure where nodes communicate what they have and what they're missing.
  - EL clients only need to support getBlobs; CLs handle the partial-message logic on top.
- Csaba (Geth) implemented message validation in go-libp2p at different levels; a blog post and slides are in preparation for the next call.
- Csaba also updated Geth's blsync CL light client to be Glamsterdam-compatible, with efficiency improvements; an experimental mode attaches to all P2P topics to fetch data directly.
  - Merged portion is the CLI light client updated for new forks; experimental P2P mode is not merged to main.
- Nethermind added a Consensus Layer plugin and plans to mesh it with P2P; also researching a light client holding partial state (per-contract or sharded across nodes) for optimization.
- No updates from Prysm (representative left before the call) or jvm-libp2p.

sections.heading: Snap ENR Entry Divergence
sections.summary: Only Geth publishes a snap key in ENR (as empty array); Chase Wright seeks cross-client consensus on whether and how to include it.
sections.body:
- Chase Wright opened [issue #286 on devp2p](https://github.com/ethereum/devp2p/issues/286) after finding that Geth is the only client publishing a `snap` key in the ENR, set as an empty array; no other client sets it.
- The EIP does not specify whether or how the snap key should be set in the ENR.
- Three proposed options: (1) don't put snap in ENR at all, (2) include snap with supported version number as the value, (3) leave it as Geth does with an empty array.
- Edge cases motivating the proposal: Reth does not support SNAP 1 but will support SNAP 2 with Amsterdam; Nimbus EL can sync snap but cannot serve snap data.
- Chase opened PRs to every EL client and a PR to devp2p to specify the proposal; a separate EIP draft update by Tony was put into draft status.
  - Nethermind already merged Chase's PR.
- No final decision on this call; Kamil will bring the issue to the Geth team for feedback. Chase asked for more client teams to comment on the issue to reach rough consensus.

sections.heading: Decoupled Consensus Simulation Results
sections.summary: Sukun presented Prysm-based and Shadow simulations showing the network can support 4× faster finality; EIP-8334 bundled attestations significantly reduce bandwidth and improve goldfish vote latency.
sections.body:
- Sukun presented simulation results from a Cambridge workshop on decoupled consensus, a proposed I-Star headliner that separates head votes (goldfish/LMD Ghost) from finality votes (Simplex/FFG).
  - [Slides and slot structure diagrams](https://github.com/ethereum/dc-networking/tree/main/personal/sukun) shared in chat.
- Approach: increase attestation subnet voting by 4× to reach finality 4× faster (target 16-slot finality); 64 committees over 64 subnets; every Beacon node subscribes to two subnets (same as today to preserve security assumptions).
- Test network: 500 cloud nodes (matching the ~447 nodes per subnet on mainnet), stubbed-out Prysm fork with correct-size objects but no real consensus logic; latest block received is treated as head.
  - 447 figure is higher than naive calculation because Prysm and Teku subscribe to aggregator duties one epoch in advance; Lighthouse subscribes only one slot in advance.
  - 2,500 validators per subnet (25% slack over the 2,000 expected on mainnet).
- **Scenario 1** (staggered FFG votes across 5-second intervals): no blocks or votes missed; payloads, data columns, goldfish votes, and blocks all arrived on time over ~200–300 slots.
  - Home node bandwidth is right at the edge: peak ~40 Mbps against a 25 Mbps limit; queues clear before next burst but votes occasionally bleed into the next slot.
  - A bug in aggregate forwarding logic (not forwarding at least one aggregate per subnet) slightly understated aggregate traffic; will be fixed.
- **Scenario 2** (Scenario 1 + EIP-8334 bundled attestations): bundling 4 attestation votes with identical head/target/source reduces 960 bytes to 552 bytes (topic name alone is 50 bytes overhead).
  - Based on partial messages; being ported to Waggle, which should yield even better numbers.
  - Arrival times improved; goldfish votes ~20% faster at P99 (730 ms vs ~1 second in Scenario 1) because slack bandwidth freed by bundling lets goldfish votes propagate without competing with FFG traffic.
  - Home node data usage well within the 25 Mbps limit with more than half the capacity remaining.
- **Scenario 3** (3 committees per subnet, published sequentially in 3-second windows): fully decouples finality traffic from availability chain; allows flexible slot alignment.
  - Goldfish votes slower (~1.2 seconds vs 1 second) due to larger burst at slot start; topic prioritization (Csaba's upcoming work) or EIP-8334 could mitigate this.
  - Numbers shown are without EIP-8334; with it, even 4-slot rounds with 8-slot finality become feasible.
- Shadow simulator results (1,000 nodes, 200 super nodes, 1M validators, 64 subnets): FFG votes propagate in time; aggregate traffic bleeds into next slot in worst case (without superset-aggregate optimization), but all objects arrive within 12-second slot.
  - Goldfish votes finish by 1.5 seconds; payload up to 2 seconds (256 KB payload; would be lower with EIP-8411).
  - This simulation represents 2× the load targeted for I-Star (8-slot finality vs. 16-slot).
- Csaba advised focusing on understanding scaling behavior (1,000 to 2,000 to 4,000 nodes) rather than running at 10,000 nodes, since the per-node load is the same; Sukun agreed.
- Anton confirmed his independent simulations show similar numbers; will compare charts in detail offline.
- Open question: staggered publishing (Scenario 1) vs. multiple committees per subnet (Scenario 3) — properties of each design need to be written down before deciding; choice currently feels arbitrary.
- Post-quantum signatures will require subnet structure changes at PQ transition; current plan is to minimize subnet changes for I-Star.

sections.heading: Zcast: Fast and Lean Broadcast Protocol
sections.summary: Csaba introduced zcast, combining segmentation, erasure coding and sampling to reach sub-700 ms latency at under 2× bandwidth overhead on 50 Mbps nodes.
sections.body:
- Csaba presented zcast (previously called Informed Diffusion), a new broadcast protocol combining techniques from FullDAS, fast chunk diffusion, Epidemic gossip, Plumtree, BitTorrent, CoolStreaming, and peer-to-peer streaming research.
  - Treats broadcast as a special case of sampled broadcast (where everyone samples the whole thing); supports both broadcast and sampled diffusion (for FullDAS/RowDAS/future ZK-proof-based block sampling).
- Key techniques: segmentation, erasure coding, fine-grained I-have/I-want control, batch publishing, and sampling — evaluated incrementally, technique by technique.
- Performance results (1 MB message):
  - Gossipsub today: high bandwidth utilization — zcast's overhead is about half of it — with latency varying by scenario (data center builder vs. home builder vs. minimum-spec network).
  - Home builders suffer significantly under current gossipsub; minimum-spec networks fail entirely.
  - Zcast achieves sub-700 ms latency on a network of 50 Mbps nodes with less than 2× bandwidth overhead (half of current gossipsub overhead).
  - Bandwidth overhead of ~1.6 copies is measured against uncompressed data; compression is applied, so effective overhead is lower.
- Zcast is elastic: under bandwidth pressure, latency increases but bandwidth utilization does not explode, avoiding critical failures that some current protocols exhibit.
- Sampled broadcast simulation: 32 blobs, 128 columns, 500 nodes, 1 Gbps source with home nodes — 50% of nodes have complete sample in ~500 ms, 100% by ~750 ms.
- Implementation: Go implementation built on go-libp2p and go-libp2p-pubsub (uses gossipsub abstractions but is not tied to gossipsub); application layer built on Prysm P2P code.
  - Also has a Python executable specification with a toy simulator; results roughly match Go implementation.
  - Simulations run on both Malco framework (native QUIC) and Shadow (TCP/QUIC backends); results match across frameworks.
- Formal modelling and verification started; some properties modeled and checked, but gaps remain (the tool named in the recording is garbled).
  - Current version is 0.5; version 0.6 in progress.
  - Byzantine resilience tested with simple withholders (up to 50%) and active malicious nodes with defined behavior in simulation; no failures observed, but not formally proven.
  - Formal verification needed to close gaps on unknown malicious behavior and guarantee system properties.
- Relationship to EIP-8411: segmentation gain is the minimum benefit; additional zcast techniques can be applied as local implementation policy on top of 8411 without protocol changes; further jumps require protocol-level changes.
- Daniel asked about scope: zcast targets single-source and multi-source diffusion (including sampled diffusion), not attestation aggregation, which involves in-network computation and many-to-many/many-to-one patterns — that would be a different protocol.
  - Could be embedded into ethp2p specifications or deployed on native QUIC for additional benefits.
- Peer scoring not the primary focus yet; short-term punishment mechanisms for non-delivery are included, but long-term scoring interaction with gossipsub-style peer scoring still being explored.
